### SUMMARY DESCRIPTION OF THE MAP OF OUR WORLD

**THE SITE** of our habitable [world] is divided into three greatest parts according to the ancients who individually scrutinized these things or who left commentaries of all these: and as we ourselves have known partly by sight, partly from their tradition. We have proposed truly to fashion a map of the whole habitable [world] so that for minds eager for learning nothing is unexperienced: and they may be able to adorn the mind through part [of it] and to compare anything through history, and to excite themselves to a certain natural sharpness. Part of our whole habitable world is bounded from the rising of the sun by unknown land which is adjacent to the eastern peoples of Greater Asia, namely the **Sinae** and the **Seres**. From the south similarly by unknown land which girds the Indian sea: or which embraces southern Ethiopia, the region called **Agisymba**. From the west also by unknown land which girds the Ethiopian gulf of Africa: and then by the western ocean which is adjacent to the furthest western parts. From the north by the ocean which then perpetually encompasses the islands of Britain and closes the most northern parts of Europe. It is called the **Deucaledonian** and **Sarmatian**. Furthermore, it has its other limits at the unknown land which looms over the most northern parts of Asia, namely **Sarmatia** and **Scythia** and the **Seres**. Furthermore, from the [equiori? perhaps *equoribus*] seas which are admitted by the land. Our sea indeed with the gulfs joined to it in the Adriatic, in the Aegean sea: in the Propontis: in the Pontus and the Maeotian marsh: exits into the ocean only through the Herculean strait [Strait of Gibraltar], making a likeness of a chersonese [peninsula]: this narrow part of the sea serves as an isthmus. The **Hyrcanian** truly which is also called the **Caspian** is surrounded on every part by land: bringing the likeness of an island from the opposite. Not otherwise do we speak of the Indian sea. For all of it with its gulfs—the Arabian, the Persian, the Gangetic, and that which by its own name is called the Great Gulf—is similarly closed by land on every part. Whence out of the three greatest parts of the whole world: Asia is joined to Africa by the ridge of Arabia which excludes our sea from the Arabian gulf; furthermore through unknown land which encompasses the Indian sea. To Europe truly it is joined through the ridge which is between the Maeotian marsh and the Sarmatian ocean in the bed of the river **Thanais**. Africa is disjoined from Europe only by the Atlantic strait [Strait of Gibraltar]; Europe by itself is in no part contiguous but through Asia especially since another [part] of them is conterminous to both: coming to meet both near their eastern quarters. Of these three, by magnitude: Asia is first. Africa second. Europe third. Similarly among the seas which are encompassed by land, as was said, by the greater space the Indian sea is first. The second sea is ours. The third the Hyrcanian or Caspian. Furthermore of the more notable gulfs: the first and similarly the greater is the Gangetic gulf. The second the Persian. The third is that which is called the Great. The fourth the Arabian. The fifth the Ethiopian. The sixth the Pontic. The seventh of the Aegean sea. The eighth of the Maeotian marsh. The ninth the Adriatic. The tenth the gulf of the Propontis. Of the more notable islands: the first is Taprobane. The second is the island of **Albion** of the Britons. The third the Golden Chersonese. The fourth Ireland of the Britons.

The fifth Peloponnesus. The sixth Sicily. The seventh Sardinia. The eighth Corsica, called Cyrnos. The ninth Crete. The tenth Cyprus. The parallel which is more southern than the equinoctial circle by 16 1/3 1/10 degrees—of those degrees such as the great circle is—bounds the southern limit of our habitable land. By the same number of degrees the parallel through **Meroe** is more northern than the equinoctial. The parallel truly most northern is bounded by that which is northern from the equinoctial by 63 degrees. This parallel truly is said [to pass] through the island of **Thyle**. Wherefore the latitude of the land known to us all consists of 79 1/3 1/10 degrees: or 80 whole degrees. In stades truly nearly forty thousand, as one degree comprises five hundred stades: as has been comprehended from more diligent dimension. The whole circuit truly consists of one hundred and eighty thousand stades. Then the meridian drawn through the metropolis of the **Sinae** bounds the extreme eastern quarter of the known world, distant from the meridian described through **Alexandria** toward the rising of the sun upon the equinoctial by 119 1/2 degrees. Nearly eight equinoctial hours truly. The meridian which is described through the **Fortunate Islands** closes the western end, and it is distant from the meridian of Alexandria by 60 1/2 degrees; four equinoctial hours truly. From the semicircle truly which is most eastern it is 180 degrees and 12 equinoctial hours. Whence it is gathered that the longitude of the whole known world upon the arc of the equinoctial circle is ninety thousand stades. Upon the most southern parallel truly eighty-six thousand and three hundred and thirty-three nearly. In the most northern parallel truly forty thousand and eight hundred and fifty-four. Again in the Rhodian parallel, in which the dimensions are especially made, distant from the equinoctial by thirty-six degrees; nearly seventy-two thousand stades. In the parallel through **Syene** which is distant from the equinoctial by 23 1/2 1/3 1/10 degrees, it truly nearly holds the middle of the whole latitude; similarly eighty-two thousand and three hundred and thirty-six according to the proportion of the aforementioned parallels to the equinoctial. Therefore the longitude of our habitable world becomes greater than the latitude in the climates which are most northern by nearly the fiftieth part of the latitude. In the climates truly through Rhodes by a certain way a half and a third part. In the climates truly which are under the parallel through **Syene** equally with the former: and nearly a sixth [part]. In the most southern quarters just as much and even nearly a sixth part. In the climates which are under the equinoctial just as much and also a quarter. The magnitude truly of the longest day or night in the parallel which is most southern has 13 equinoctial hours. Similarly in the parallel through **Meroe**.

### DESCRIPTION OF THE CIRCULAR SPHERE WITH THE HABITABLE LAND

**AS** above written are the things concerning the universal disposition of the site as far as here with equal dimension. It is not truly incongruous to add to these in what way the hemisphere of the earth which is shown can be described in a plane contained under a circular sphere. Since therefore many have labored to show this and have used this demonstration most absurdly, let it be proposed that a circular sphere is to be described in a plane with the earth comprehended within. Let the aspect of the eye therefore have a site through which a straight line is made in all sections: the meridian which passes through the signs of the tropics: and which cuts the longitude of the habitable land: and the parallel noted in the earth through **Syene** dividing also this latitude of the habitable [world]. Thus truly let the ratios of the magnitudes of the circular sphere and the earth and the absence of the aspect itself be held as in the distance which is gathered between the circle near the equinoctial and the summer tropic; the whole part of the world known to us appears with the more southern semicircle established upon the earth through the middle circle of the Zodiac: lest beyond it any addition be made of the habitable [world] itself to the northern hemisphere in [leptense? possibly *latenesse* or *extense*]. Because therefore under these said [conditions] the meridians of one straight line according to it.

***

### PAGE 141
**[[Original page 68]]**

**<- VII ->**

...they provide an axis of the imagination: as if by the very sight of them, these same things [appear] to you in a plane; and that the parallel of **Syenes** is at a right angle to those, and by similar reasoning the rest which are described as bent in the manner of arcs toward the straight lines themselves should appear: the meridians [bent] toward the line that passes through the poles, but the parallels toward that which passes through **Syene**; and that these [meridians] are more distant from them on either side, as is manifest from that place.

How, however, I shall show: by a description as similar as possible to the image, it will be easy for our eyes in this manner. Let the meridian which passes through the equinoctial signs in the circular sphere be *a b c d* around center *e* and diameter *a e c*; and let us understand *a* indeed to be at the Arctic pole, and *c* at the Antarctic. And let the circumferences *b f* and *d g* and *b h* and *d k* be taken at the distances of the tropics from the equinoctial; or *a l* and *a m* and *n c* and *c o* at the distances of the Arctic and Antarctic poles. And let the diameter of the summer [tropic] *a e* be divided according to *p*. Since, therefore, it is necessary for the parallel through **Syene** to be situated between *e* and *p*, and the ratio of the circumference from the parallel of **Syenes** to the equinoctial to the quadrant—that is, nearly four to five—and the middle part of *e p* to *e a* is nearly four to fifteen of the same parts: *e a* will be the sesquitertian [*epitritus*] of the line going out from the center of the earth.

Let *e q* be assumed, however, of three such parts as *e a* is of four; and from center *e* with the distance *e p*, let a circle *q r* be described which encompasses the earth in the same plane. And a certain straight line having been divided equal to *e q* into ninety equal portions in one quadrant: namely, there remain 63 portions of *e p*. And *e f* consists of 16 5/12 portions. And *e t* of 63 of the same. And let *x f y* be drawn to fall upon the straight line, clearly following the parallel of **Syenes**: there will be, therefore, *f q* from *p*, by which shall be inscribed the parallel cutting the southern boundary of the habitable world and opposite to the parallel through **Meroe**. And *v p*, by which shall be inscribed the Arctic parallel terminating the description through **Thyle**. And let something more southern than *c* be taken, such as *z*, and let *z a* be joined, and *f y* and *z d* be extended and coincide at *ll*.

If, therefore, we understand the set-out circles in a plane through the signs of the tropics and the poles, and the aspect of the eye from *ll*, the lines extended from *p m g d k* and *o e* to *a c* will make five sections of the parallels toward *z p*, by which will be inscribed that which is the equinoctial around *d*. Those, however, which are joined from *ll* to *d* and *b* and *f* and *h* and *g* will make the same section, namely at *a c*, through which the boundaries of the earth and the portions of the same parallels shall be inscribed. Similarly, however, in describing the parallels on the earth, taking the proper absences from the equinoctial on *q r* such as *z* and *t*, we will have the sections made by the same joined straight lines from *ll* of the semicircle *q y r* itself, and the sections to be described opposite to them according to equidistant sites for the view of the eye. Five parallels toward *ll*, through which will be inscribed that equinoctial which is around *d*. Those, however, which are joined from *ll* to *d* and *b* and *f* and *h* and *g* make the same sections at *c* through the portions of the said parallels, such as *a t b* and *c t d*. From which, taking the distances of the ordered meridians on either side from *v* and *m x y* in a straight line, in the proper ratios of the three parallels, we shall write through three similar points the subject portions of the meridians, as if terminating the longitude *e y f g* and *p g*.

The multitude of things to be described on the earth must be adapted to the description of the magnitude. In the drawing of the circles, however, this must be observed: that each should proceed by taking four signs, and in the painting, it should not end in a sharp point at the section of the outermost circle, lest it induce a phantasy contrary to order; but even here, a consistency is to be held toward those things which follow, although the cities might fall outside the circle containing the painting itself, finishing those defects with the circle which in the true image itself appeared to fall.

It must also be noticed that the lines themselves are circles with a certain commensurable width and different color. Moreover, that the portions which are placed beyond the earth should have darker colors; and those portions which are offered to the sight, and also those more remote from the sight, should be cut by the coincident portions from the nearer ones, together with the additions of true images in the circles themselves and the earth itself; besides this, that the circle of the signs [the zodiac] falls upon the earth, which proceeds according to the more southern semicircle and through the winter tropic. Let it be cut, however, by it according to the northern part and through the summer tropic itself. Let us also ascribe to these, in the more opportune places, their proper names, and in the circles of the earth itself, the numbers of the distances and the hours of the habitable world itself.

### PAGE 142
**[[Original page L]]**

Around the outer circle, we shall likewise place the names of the winds, just as in the circular sphere at the adjacent five parallels and the poles themselves.

**EPILOGUE OF THE AFOREMENTIONED EXTENSION**

An epilogue of this extension will seem appropriate here. A circular description of the sphere in a plane, with the earth included in the same, will be had if the aspect of our eye is fixed in a position according to which, in the common sections, the meridian circle proceeding through the points of the tropics becomes a straight line, which divides the circle of our habitable world in longitude. Moreover, the parallel described through **Syene**, which circle divides the latitude of the habitable world almost equally.

Thus, however, let the ratios of the magnitudes of the sphere and the earth itself, and the distance of the sight itself, be held so that in the space which lies between the circle near the equinoctial and the circle near the summer tropic, the whole known habitable world appears to us, with the southern semicircle of the signs established through the middle over the earth; lest under this, some addition of our habitable world be made which might extend to the Arctic hemisphere. From which it is said that the meridians, according to the axis itself, will produce the phantasy of a single straight line, as if the aspect itself were falling through them onto a plane; and the parallel which is inscribed through **Syene** may also appear straight for a similar reason.

The rest of the circles to be noted truly appear toward those straight lines through the cities: the meridians toward those which pass through the poles, the parallels truly toward those which through **Syene** are more distant there than on either side. So that the circle more Arctic than the summer tropic inclines more toward the North [*Arcton*]. The winter tropic truly more than the equinoctial: which is more inclined toward the south. Moreover, the Antarctic circle more than the winter tropic itself. The known part of the earth itself has its site as the Ocean, which itself surrounds it on no part except only in the boundaries described in the reaches on the side of **Affrica** and **Europe**, according to the traditions of the ancients.

**THE SEVENTH BOOK OF CLAUDIUS PTOLEMY’S COSMOGRAPHY ENDS**

**THE EIGHTH AND LAST BOOK OF THE COSMOGRAPHY OF CLAUDIUS PTOLEMY, MAN OF ALEXANDRIA, BEGINS**

With which presupposition it is necessary to make the division of our habitable world into tables [maps].
What is fitting to adapt to each table.
An exposition of all the summaries in which are contained:
In **Europe**, ten tables: thirty-four provinces.
In **Affrica**, four tables: twelve provinces.
In Great **Asia**, twelve tables: forty-eight provinces.

**WITH WHICH PRESUPPOSITION IT IS NECESSARY TO MAKE THE DIVISION OF OUR HABITABLE WORLD INTO TABLES**

Whatever indeed was necessary for the work of cosmography, partly from the diligent care of those who have traveled through our regions, and partly from the consideration held for a simultaneously easier and more proper [method], I judge to have been sufficiently explained. But just as the examples of our predecessors warn, namely that through an epilogue it should be repeated through which places each parallel and meridian is noted in our table: lest it become ridiculous that all places simply, even those not falling under the set-out circles and having distances lying between the parallels and meridians themselves, be placed confusedly.

Since it has been shown in what manner the description of our whole habitable world contained in one table might be commensurable to the sight of the eyes, it remains to demonstrate summarily the future descriptions: if we divide that table into several tables so that all explored places can be arranged with a clearer and certain commensuration. Since, therefore, one table is necessary, because it is necessary to observe equality to the sites of the other parts: some [must be] compressed on account of the frequency of places; others extended...

***

### PAGE 143
**[[Original page 69]]**

**<- VIII ->**

...on account of the scarcity, just as many have been forced to do more carelessly and in many ways pervert [them] in the tables themselves: under the measures and figures of the regions, lest they seem to have departed from history. As those who assigned the greatest part of the table to **Europe** according to longitude and latitude because more frequent sites and places had to be placed in it. They left, however, the smallest space to **Asia** according to longitude and likewise to **Affrica** according to latitude for a reason diverse from the former; for which cause they deflected the Indian sea after **Taprobanem** toward the north, since the table itself suggested a bare space toward the progress to the rising of the sun; and they had nothing to describe in **Scythia** toward the north.

They turned the western ocean truly to the eastern region, since the table equally exceeded them in distance to the meridian, while the vastness of **Affrica** or **India** had nothing frequent and continuous which could be opposed to the western shore from a similar frequency of places. Whence, so that they might gird the globe on all sides with the ocean, imbued with an opinion of this kind: they began with a deceptive description to turn to history with an uncomposed and inept painting.

By the partition of the table, therefore, we shall be able to avoid this error if we divide it so that the regions more frequent with places—which alone or with a few others obtain one table—[are drawn] with greater distances of the circles. Those truly less inhabited and occupied by fewer sites, are contained with many similar ones under one table in smaller distances of the circles. For it is not necessary here that all tables be equally commensurable simultaneously: but that each alone in any single [case] preserves the proportion. Just as when we describe a single head: which are of the head alone; as when a single hand, which are of the hand alone; nor do we figure those which are of the head and the hand simultaneously, except when we make the whole man under one figure. Whence, just as nothing hinders sometimes diminishing a certain whole; so in the parts, when they are disjoined, we can both increase them individually and diminish them according to the frequency of places to be noted in our tables.

Nor will it be far from the truth, as we said at the beginning of the work, if we describe straight lines instead of circles. Moreover, in the particular tables we shall note the meridians themselves not inclined and bent: but mutually equidistant. Since, however, in the whole habitable world, the boundaries of latitude and longitude taken according to great distances do not make certain significant excesses in the extreme circles, nor in any of the tables. Then, since we say it is fitting for comparisons of degrees to be made according to the proportion of the parallel dividing the table to the greatest circle: we do not seek that also for the whole distance of the table, but only that which is distant from one extreme to the other extreme.

**WHAT IS FITTING TO ADAPT TO EACH TABLE**

These things therefore having been presupposed, approaching a division of this kind, we shall establish ten tables of **Europe**. Four tables of **Affrica**. Twelve tables of all **Asia**. In any table, however, we shall add a certain summary, prefixing what the table you are establishing is: and how large it is, and what regions or provinces it has: and what ratio the parallel has which moves through its middle, which can be done more certainly to the meridian itself: and what the circumscription of the whole table becomes: subordinating through each region the assumed elevations of the notable cities to the magnitude of the longest days in them.

We shall take the distance truly according to longitude through the absences from the meridian through **Alexandria**, whether to the rising of the sun or to the setting, from the magnitude or number of the equinoctial hours. Moreover, over which [places] the circle of the signs [zodiac] lies: and over which once or twice the sun becomes directly overhead [at the zenith]: and in what way it has its site toward the tropics themselves. We would also have added which [stars] it has overhead if the latitudes toward the equinoctial itself appeared by observation—that is, if they were always led through the same parallels. Since, however, I showed...

***

### PAGE 144

...in the mathematical work [*the Almagest*] that the sphere of the fixed stars is revolved toward the consequent revolutions of the orb, and [revolved] by the equinoctial signs, nor around the poles of the equinoctial, but around the poles of the circle proceeding through the middle of the zodiac; just as in the erratic [planets], the same stars cannot always be above the zenith of the same places, but are necessarily transferred, some to more northern places than before, others truly more southern.

Such an addition of an epilogue would have been in vain, since it is permitted in the sphere of the stars according to this hypothesis, in any of its times, by establishing its site toward the circle of both poles and revolving the whole to the divided side of the permanent meridian: to consider the sign itself absent by as many degrees from the equinoctial as the parallel itself of the sought place. Which will easily be done through both poles; by no means will any place be withdrawn; through that sign of the fixed stars, whether many or for which some. These things therefore having been pre-defined, those things which remain must be begun.

**HENCE FOLLOW THE TABLES**

Around the outer circle, we will likewise add the names of the winds, just as in a circular sphere relative to the five adjacent <term>parallels</term><note>Lines of latitude</note> and the poles themselves.

### EPILOGUE TO THE AFOREMENTIONED PROJECTION

**H**ere, an epilogue to this projection will seem fitting. A description of a circular sphere on a plane, with the earth included within it, will be achieved if our eye's gaze is fixed at a point where, in common sections, the <term>meridian</term><note>A line of longitude</note> circle passing through the points of the tropics becomes a straight line; this is the circle that divides our inhabited world by its length. Furthermore, the parallel drawn through **Syene**<note>Modern-day Aswan, Egypt; used by ancient geographers as a key reference point for the Tropic of Cancer</note> also acts as a divider, splitting the latitude of the inhabited world almost equally. 

Thus, the ratios of the sizes of the sphere and the earth itself, and the distance of the gaze, should be held such that in the space lying between the circle near the equator and the circle near the summer tropic, the entire known inhabited world appears to us. This is done by placing the more southern semicircle over the earth through the middle of the <term>zodiac</term><note>original: "circalu signorum"; the path of the sun through the constellations</note>, lest some addition to our inhabited world be made beneath this which might extend into the Arctic hemisphere. From this, it is said that the meridians, following the axis itself, will create the illusion of a single straight line, as if the gaze itself falls on them in a flat plane. For a similar reason, the parallel drawn through **Syene** also appears as a straight line. 

The rest of the circles to be noted truly appear as curves relative to those straight lines: the meridians [curve] toward those that pass through the poles, while the parallels curve toward the one passing through **Syene**. In those regions, they are further apart than on either side. Thus, the Arctic circle leans more toward the north than the summer tropic does. The winter tropic, however, leans more than the equatorial circle, being more inclined toward the south. Furthermore, the Antarctic circle leans more than the winter tropic itself. The known part of the earth is positioned such that the ocean does not surround it on any side, except only at the boundaries described in the coastal regions of **Africa** and **Europe**, according to the traditions of the elders.

->**HERE ENDS THE SEVENTH BOOK OF CLAUDIUS PTOLEMY’S COSMOGRAPHY**<-

->**THE EIGHTH AND FINAL BOOK OF THE COSMOGRAPHY OF CLAUDIUS PTOLEMY, MAN OF ALEXANDRIA, BEGINS**<-

This book contains:
*   The premise required to divide our inhabited world into individual maps.
*   What features are suitable to adapt to each map.
*   An exposition of all the summaries contained within: In **Europe**, ten maps and thirty-four provinces. In **Africa**, four maps and twelve provinces. In **Greater Asia**, twelve maps and forty-eight provinces.

### WITH WHAT PREMISE IT IS NECESSARY TO MAKE THE DIVISION OF OUR INHABITED WORLD INTO MAPS

**W**hatever has been necessary for the work of <term>cosmography</term><note>The science of mapping the general features of the universe and earth</note>—derived partly from the diligent study of those who have traveled through our regions, and partly from considerations held for a simpler and more appropriate method—I think has been sufficiently explained. 

However, as the examples of our predecessors suggest, we should provide an epilogue to repeat through which places each parallel and meridian noted in our map is located. This is to avoid a ridiculous result: where all places, especially those not falling directly under the established circles but lying in the distances between the parallels and meridians, are placed in a confused manner. Since it has already been shown how the description of our entire inhabited world can be contained in a single map proportional to the eye's view, it remains to demonstrate in summary the future descriptions. We shall do this by dividing that large map into several smaller maps, so that all explored places can be arranged with a clearer and more certain proportion. 

While a single map is necessary to maintain the correct relationship between the positions of all parts, other maps must be constricted because of the high density of locations, while others are extended...

<meta>This page transitions from the general theory of map projection to the practical organization of regional maps. <- VIII ->

...your lack [of space], just as many have been forced to act less carefully and compress many things poorly on the maps themselves, under the measurements and shapes of the regions, so that they would not seem to have departed from history. For instance, those who assigned the largest part of the map to **Europe** in terms of both length and width, simply because more sites and locations had to be placed within it. However, they left the smallest space for **Asia** in terms of length, and likewise for **Africa** in terms of width, for the opposite reason. Because of this, they deflected the **Indian Sea** northward after **Taprobane**<note>Modern-day Sri Lanka; ancient geographers often exaggerated its size and debated its exact location</note>, even though the map itself suggested an empty space for progress toward the rising sun, and they had nothing to describe in **Scythia** toward the north. 

They even turned the Western Ocean toward the eastern region, although the map equally exceeded the distance to the south for them, since the vastness of **Africa** or **India** had nothing frequent or continuous that could be placed opposite the western shore, based on a similar frequency of locations. From this, being imbued with the opinion that they should encircle the world on all sides with an ocean, they began to turn toward a history of disorganized and inept pictures with a deceptive description. We will be able to avoid this error in the division of the map if we divide it so that the regions with more locations—whether alone or with a few others—receive a single map with larger distances between the <term>circles</term><note>Here referring to the lines of the coordinate grid</note>. Conversely, those regions that are less inhabited and occupied by fewer sites should be contained with several similar ones under one map, with smaller distances between the circles. 

For it is not necessary here that all maps be equally commensurable with one another at the same time; rather, it is only necessary that each individual map preserves its own proportion. Just as when we describe only a head, we depict what belongs to the head alone; or when we draw only a hand, what belongs to the hand alone; we do not figure the head and hand together [at the same scale] unless we are making the whole man under a single figure. Hence, just as nothing prevents us from sometimes shrinking a whole, so too in the parts, when they are separated, we can both enlarge them individually and shrink them according to the frequency of locations to be noted on the maps. 

Nor will it be far from the truth, as we said at the beginning of the work, if we describe straight lines instead of circles <gloss>curved arcs</gloss> for these maps. Furthermore, in these particular maps, we will mark the <term>meridians</term><note>Lines of longitude</note> themselves not as inclined or curved, but as equally distant from each other. However, when the boundaries of latitude and longitude in the entire inhabited world are taken according to the large distances, they do not create any significant excesses in the outer circles, nor in any of the maps. Then, since we say the comparisons of degrees ought to be made according to the proportion of the <term>parallel</term><note>Line of latitude</note> dividing the map to the <term>great circle</term><note>The Equator</note>, we should not seek that for the entire distance of the map, but only for that which lies from one extreme to the other.

<- WHAT IS APPROPRIATE TO ADAPT TO EACH MAP ->

**H**aving therefore presupposed these things, and approaching this kind of division, we shall establish **ten maps for Europe**. **Four maps for Africa**. **Twelve maps for the whole of Asia**. 

In each map, we will add a certain summary, setting forth what the map is that you are establishing, and how large it is, and what regions or provinces it contains. We will also state the ratio of the parallel that passes through its middle, which can be done more accurately in relation to the meridian itself, and what the circumference of the entire map should be. We shall subordinate, through each region, the elevations <gloss>latitudes</gloss> of the notable cities, taken according to the length of their longest days. We will take the distance according to longitude through the departures from the meridian through **Alexandria**<note>Alexandria served as the "prime meridian" for Ptolemy, the zero-point from which all eastern and western distances were measured</note>, whether toward the rising of the sun <gloss>East</gloss> or toward its setting <gloss>West</gloss>, based on the size or number of <term>equinoctial hours</term><note>Hours of equal length, regardless of the season, used for astronomical and geographical calculations</note>. Furthermore, we will note which signs of the zodiac lie above them, and for which ones the sun is directly overhead <gloss>at the zenith</gloss> once or twice, and how it is positioned relative to the **tropics** themselves. We would also have added which latitudes they would have overhead if, by observation, they appeared in relation to the **equinoctial** <gloss>Equator</gloss> itself—that is, if they were always led through the same parallels. However, as I was showing...

<meta>This page concludes the introductory or theoretical section of the work, focusing on how celestial movements—specifically the precession of the stars—affect geographical coordinates. It transitions from these astronomical proofs into the "Tables" (maps and coordinate lists) that form the core of the atlas.</meta>

...in a mathematical work, because the sphere of the **fixed stars**<note>The "fixed stars" (stellae fixae) are the stars that appear to stay in the same position relative to one another, as opposed to "wandering stars" or planets.</note> is turned according to the revolving motions of the world, and not according to the <term>equinoctial signs</term><note>Signs of the zodiac relative to the equator.</note> nor around the <term>equinoctial</term><note>The celestial equator.</note> poles, but rather around the poles of the circle moving through the middle of the **zodiac**. Just as with the wandering stars, the same stars cannot always be directly above the same locations; instead, they are necessarily moved, some to more northern locations than before, and others to more southern ones.

It would have been useless to add such a concluding summary, since within the sphere of the stars—following this hypothesis—it is possible at any time to establish its position relative to the circle of both poles. By rotating the whole sphere against the divided edge of a permanent <term>meridian</term><note>A line of longitude; here referring to a physical part of a globe or instrument used for measurement.</note>, one can observe the star's position, noting it is as many degrees distant from the equator as the parallel of the location in question. This can easily be observed through both poles so that no place is overlooked; through that sign of the fixed stars, or several of them. Therefore, these things having been defined, the remaining matters must be begun.

### **The Surrounding Oceans**
*   **The Hyperborean Ocean** <note>original: "OCEANVS IPERBOREVS." This refers to the far northern waters, named after the mythical people who lived "beyond the North Wind."</note>
*   **The Deucaledonian Ocean** <note>original: "OCEANVS DVE CALLEDONIVS." The sea to the north of Scotland.</note>

### Translator's Notes on Abbreviations and Technical Terms:

1.  **Abbreviations:**
    *   *cũ* → *cum* (with)
    *   *proportionē* → *proportionem* (proportion/ratio)
    *   *fretroqꝙ* → *fretoque* (and the strait)
    *   *pꝑte* → *parte* (part/region)
    *   *horarū/horarū* → *horarum* (of hours)
    *   *diē* → *diem* (day)
2.  **Fractional Notation:** In the city data section, the OCR utilizes fractions (1/2, 2/3, 1/12, etc.) to represent the subdivisions of hours (minutes) according to Ptolemaic geographic tradition. For example, "14 1/2 1/12" indicates 14 hours and 35 minutes.
3.  **Proper Nouns:** As per instructions, the Latin forms of place names (e.g., *Betica*, *Tarraconensis*, *Gadira*) have been retained.
4.  **Climata:** These refer to the ancient system of latitudinal bands based on the duration of the longest day.
5.  **Unclear Reading:** The OCR for Page 151 lists "Cluma"; this is a common typographic variation or error for **CLVNIA** (Clunia Sulpicia).

# **BOOK THREE**

## *Concerning Navigation and Hydrography*

<margin>Chapter 1.</margin>
In this third book, after we have spoken of Cosmography and Astronomy, we approach the art of sailing. *Navigation* is the science by which a journey is directed safely and correctly across the sea. A <term>rhumb line</term> <note>original: "loxodromia"</note> is a curved line on a sphere that intersects all meridians at a constant angle. <note>In navigation, a rhumb line allows a sailor to maintain a constant compass heading, though it is not the shortest distance between two points on a globe.</note>

Four things are necessary for the sailor:
1. A sea chart.
2. The magnet and compass. <note>The original text refers to the "magnes" (magnet) and "pyxis" (the box or casing), which together form the mariner's compass.</note>
3. The astrolabe. <note>An ancient instrument used to determine latitude by measuring the altitude of the sun or stars.</note>
4. Tables of movements. <note>These are astronomical tables, such as ephemerides, used to calculate the positions of celestial bodies for navigation.</note>

->*Table of Winds*<-

| Name | Angle |
| :--- | :--- |
| North | 0° |
| East | 90° |
| South | 180° |
| West | 270° |

<gloss>Here begins the practical part.</gloss>

<summary>This page marks the beginning of Book Three, shifting the focus from theoretical cosmology to the practical science of navigation and hydrography. It defines navigation, introduces the concept of the rhumb line, and lists the essential tools required for a mariner.</summary>

<keywords>navigation, hydrography, rhumb line, compass, astrolabe, nautical instruments, wind directions</keywords>

**Scholarly Notes on the Transcription:**
1.  **Abbreviations:** The symbol `ꝑ` is a standard scribal abbreviation for *per*. The form `hīs` is used here for *habens* (having). `hōꝝ` represents *horarum* (of hours). 
2.  **Fractions:** In the city coordinates (e.g., *14 2/2 1/4*), the "2/2" is an OCR artifact or a specific typesetting for the fraction $1/2$. In Ptolemaic geography, these denote the length of the longest day, which determines the latitude.
3.  **Climates (*Climata*):** These refer to the ancient Greek system of dividing the earth into seven latitudinal zones based on the duration of the longest day.
4.  **Toponyms:** *Mediolanum* in Aquitaine refers to *Mediolanum Santonum* (modern Saintes), not the more famous Milan in Italy.

### Translator’s Notes on Abbreviations and Readings:
1. **[abbrev: ꝙ → quod]**: This is a standard scribal abbreviation for "quod."
2. **uſus**: The OCR identifies this as "uſus," but in Renaissance geographical shorthand, it is a contraction for *versus* (towards).
3. **Fractions**: Latitude and longitude are expressed in hours. Ptolemy often uses composite fractions (e.g., 1/2 1/3) which are additive.
4. **Equinoctial**: Refers to the Equator.
5. **Clima**: Ptolemy divided the known world into seven "Climata" or zones based on the length of the longest day.
6. **Alexandridia**: Likely a typographical error in the original for *Alexandria*.
7. **quid parū**: (*quiddam parvum*) "a small amount more."
8. **occaſus occaſum**: A textual redundancy/error in the original OCR/print; likely intended to be simply *versus occasum*.
9. **Narbona**: Not to be confused with Narbonne in France; here referring to *Naro* or *Narona* in Dalmatia.
10. **hadi ma.**: Abbreviation for *habens diem maiorem* (having the longest day).
11. **14 1/2 1/3**: Note that 1/2 + 1/3 = 5/6, making the day 14 hours and 50 minutes.

# THE FIFTH MAP OF EUROPE
<note>This decorative initial **V** marks the beginning of the description for the fifth regional map in Ptolemy's series, covering the central and southeastern Alpine and Balkan regions.</note>

This map contains **Rhaetia**, **Vindelicia**, and **Noricum**, the two **Pannonias**, and all of **Illyria**, along with the adjacent islands. Its middle parallel has a ratio to the meridian of forty-three to sixty <note>This ratio was used by ancient cartographers to account for the curvature of the Earth when flattening a map; it determines how much narrower the degrees of longitude are compared to degrees of latitude at this specific distance from the equator.</note>. The map is bounded on the **East** by the Iazyges Metanastae and Upper Moesia; on the **South** by Italy and the Adriatic Gulf along the side of Macedonia; and on the **North** by Greater Germany.

**NOTABLE CITIES OF RHAETIA**
<note>Rhaetia was a Roman province encompassing parts of modern-day eastern Switzerland, Austria, and Bavaria.</note>
**Brigantium** <note>Modern-day Bregenz, Austria.</note> has a longest day of 15 2/3 hours and is 2 hours distant from Alexandria toward the west.

### PAGE 187

**THERE ARE VERY MANY**
regions which indeed seem to excel each in their own individual things. For **Arabia** alone produces frankincense. Balsam is gathered nowhere except in **Iudea**; ivory comes from **India**. Likewise, we receive other things from other nations. Truly, if you should judge all things most exactly, you will surely find that **Italia** is by right to be preferred above all. For if you recall the ancient kings in her, she was made illustrious by **Saturnus** and **Ianus**, kings of whom one handed down the discipline not only of cultivating the fields, but also of many other things. **Ianus**, however, taught sacred ceremonies and the highest piety toward the immortal gods.

**Italia** was always so powerful in military affairs that at no time did she exist without a splendid empire. For the power of the **Umbri** was by no means small; the **Tirreri** succeeded the **Umbri**, of whom it is most clearly shown that they ruled the whole of **Italia** by the fact that the Upper Sea was named **Adriaticum** from their colony **Adria**, while the Lower Sea was named **Tirrenum** from the people themselves. After the **Etrusci**, the **Latini** took up the empire, the nature and greatness of which all men know. 

But indeed, there was no people in her who did not excel in some thing. For what is more affluent than the **Calabrian** and the **Appulian**? What more noble than the **Campanian**? What proved more populous than the **Sannite**? Among the **Sabini** there was the greatest severity and sanctity. To the **Etrusci** nothing was lacking that pertains to religion. In the **Ligures** there appeared a great patience for all labors and difficulties. 

But these things concern the men. As for the site of the place: what could be devised more suited for healthfulness, or more fit for all utilities, or more pleasant for delight? For the climate is such that it neither thins the bodies with excessive subtlety, nor corrupts them with excessive thickness. And it is so tempered between cold and heat that the poet [4] most truly said: *Here is perpetual spring and summer in months not its own.* It possesses, moreover, two seas—the Upper, as I have said, and the Lower—through which, by very frequent and safest ports, whatever things are of use to the human race may be imported and exported. It also has navigable and fish-filled rivers and lakes; and though the hills are clothed with trees and the fields with crops, nevertheless the **Appenninus** mountain is perpetual, dividing **Italia**, which both brings beauty by this distinction and abundantly provides timber from the rivers for the use of all.

Therefore, since this region—both for these reasons I have mentioned and especially because it has always been the head of nations, formerly on account of the monarchy of the **Romani** and now on account of the **Apostolic See**—I have decided to describe more diffusely, setting aside the names of the nations which have now been recited by **Ptolemeus**, according to our times: the cities, towns, lakes, shores, ports, and mountains; also the names of the rivers and their origins, as well as the mountainous and level places, together with the islands adjacent to them, as is right to behold; transgressing in nothing those things which were observed by the author of this book with certain dimension and most true reckoning.

# THE SEVENTH MAP OF EUROPE
The map contains the islands of **Sardinia** and **Sicily**. Its middle parallel has a proportion to the meridian of four to five. <note>This refers to the map's projection; for every 5 units of latitude (north-south), there are 4 units of longitude (east-west), accounting for the curvature of the Earth at this latitude.</note> The map is bounded on all sides by the sea: from the east by the Adriatic <note>original: "hadriatico"</note>; from the south by the African sea; from the west by the Sardinian sea; and from the north by the Ligurian sea.

## FAMOUS CITIES OF THE ISLAND OF SARDINIA
**Sufaleos** <note>Likely Usellus</note> has its longest day at 14 1/2 1/12 hours <note>Ancient geographers defined latitude by the length of the longest day of the year; 14 hours and 35 minutes corresponds to approximately 39° North.</note> and is distant from Alexandria toward the west by 1 1/2 1/3 1/4 hours. <note>Ptolemy measured longitude in time; 1 hour equals 15 degrees. These fractions are additive: 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/4 = 2 hours and 5 minutes.</note>

**Caralis** <note>modern Cagliari</note> has its longest day at 14 1/2 hours and is distant from Alexandria toward the west by 1 1/2 1/3 hours.

**Turris Libisonis** <note>original: "Turris biffonis," modern Porto Torres</note> has its longest day at 14 1/2 hours and is distant from Alexandria toward the west by nearly 1/2 hour.

**Gurullis Nova** <note>modern Cuglieri</note> has its longest day at 14 1/2 1/8 hours and is distant from Alexandria toward the west by 1 1/2 1/3 1/8 hours.

## FAMOUS CITIES OF THE ISLAND OF SICILY
Truly in Sicily, **Lilybaeum** <note>modern Marsala</note> has its longest day at 14 1/2 hours and is distant from Alexandria toward the west by 1 1/2 1/4 hours.

**Syracuse** has its longest day at 14 1/2 1/8 hours and is distant from Alexandria toward the west by 1 1/3 1/4 hours.

**Messina** <note>original: "Mesena"</note> has its longest day at 14 1/2 1/4 hours and is distant from Alexandria toward the west by 1 1/3 1/8 hours.

**Segesta** has its longest day at 14 1/4 hours (and a little bit) and is distant from Alexandria toward the west by 1 1/2 1/4 hours.

**Catania** <note>original: "Catana"</note> has its longest day at 14 1/3 hours and is distant from Alexandria toward the west by 1 1/3 1/4 hours.

# THERE ARE MANY
regions that indeed seem each to excel in individual things. <note>The author begins with a classical rhetorical device, comparing Italy's virtues to the specialized products of other famous lands.</note> For Arabia alone produces frankincense. Balsam is gathered nowhere but in Judea; ivory comes from India. Likewise, we receive other things from different nations. But if you judge all things most accurately, you will surely find that Italy is by every right to be preferred above all. For if you recall the ancient kings in that land, it was made illustrious by the kings **Saturn** and **Janus** <note>In Roman mythology, Saturn was a primordial deity who taught men agriculture, while Janus was the god of beginnings, often depicted with two faces.</note>: the one of whom handed down the discipline not only of cultivating the fields, but also of many other things. **Janus**, however, taught sacred ceremonies and the highest piety toward the immortal gods.

Italy was always so powerful in military affairs that there was never any time without a **splendid empire**. For the power of the **Umbrians** was not least; the **Tyrrhenians** <note>The Tyrrhenians are the people known today as the Etruscans.</note> succeeded the Umbrians, of whom it is most clearly declared that they ruled all of Italy by the fact that the **Upper Sea** <note>The Adriatic Sea.</note> was named "Adriatic" from their colony, Adria, while the **Lower Sea** was called "**Tyrrhenian**" <note>The Tyrrhenian Sea, bordering Italy's western coast.</note> from the people themselves. After the Etruscans, the **Latins** took up the empire, the quality and greatness of which all men know. 

But indeed there was no people in Italy who did not excel in some way. For what was more affluent than the **Calabrian** and **Apulian**? What more noble than the **Campanian**? What lived more populous than the **Samnite**? Among the **Sabines** there was the greatest austerity and sanctity. To the **Etruscans**, nothing was lacking that pertains to religion. In the **Ligurians**, the greatest patience for all labors and difficulties appeared. 

But these things concern the men. As for the site of the place: what can be thought of that is either more accommodated to health, or more suited to all uses, or more pleasant for delight? For the sky is of such a kind that it neither thins the bodies with excessive subtlety nor corrupts them with excessive thickness. And it is so tempered between cold and heat that the poet <note>The author is quoting the Roman poet Virgil, from his work *Georgics*, Book 2.</note> most truly said: *Here is perpetual spring and summer in months not its own.* <note>original: "Hic ver perpetuum atque alienis mensibus estas"</note> It has, moreover, two seas—the **Upper**, as I said, and the **Lower**—through which, with very frequent and safe ports, whatever things are of use to the human race may be imported and exported. It also has navigable and fish-filled rivers and lakes; and while the hills are clothed with trees and the fields with crops, there is nonetheless the continuous **Apennine** mountain range dividing Italy; it brings beauty through this distinction, and from its streams, it provides an abundance of timber for the use of all. 

Therefore, because of these reasons I have stated, and especially because it has always been the head of nations—formerly due to the **Roman Monarchy** and now due to the **Apostolic See** <note>The "Apostolic See" refers to the Papacy and the spiritual authority of Rome in the Christian world.</note>—I have decided (leaving aside the names of nations now recited by Ptolemy) to describe more diffusely the cities, towns, lakes, shores, ports, and mountains of our own times, as well as the names of rivers and their sources, and also the mountainous and level places, together with the islands adjacent to them, as is right to behold. In doing so, I shall not transgress in any of those things which were observed with certain dimension and most true reasoning by the author of this book <note>The "author" refers to Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century geographer whose work forms the basis of this atlas.</note>.

<summary>This page serves as a celebratory preface to the description of Italy, praising its history, climate, and geography. The author justifies updating Ptolemy's ancient data with contemporary Renaissance details, citing Italy's status as the center of both the Roman Empire and the Catholic Church.</summary>

<keywords>Italy, Saturn, Janus, Etruscans, Roman Empire, Papacy, Apennines, Adriatic Sea, Tyrrhenian Sea, Virgil, geography</keywords>

### Scholarly Notes on the Translation:

1.  **Abbreviations:** The text uses standard Renaissance abbreviations. *Maximā diē hēt* is *Maximam diem habet* ("Has its longest day"). *ūſus* is a common shorthand for *versus* ("towards"). *q̃* is *quae* and *q_* is the enclitic *-que*.
2.  **Fractional Notation:** Ptolemy's coordinates were often expressed in vulgar fractions (e.g., 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/8, 1/12). In some instances, multiple fractions are listed together (e.g., 14 3/12 1/2), which usually implies an addition of the parts to reach a specific degree or minute.
3.  **Geographical Concepts:**
    *   **Maximā diē (Longest Day):** In ancient geography, latitude was often expressed by the length of the longest day of the year at that location.
    *   **Dīſtat ab alexādria (Distance from Alexandria):** Longitude was measured as a time difference from the prime meridian of Alexandria.
    *   **Middle Parallel:** The ratio provided (e.g., 11 to 20) refers to the mathematical projection used to draw the map, comparing the length of a degree of longitude at that specific latitude to a degree of latitude on the equator.
4.  **Proper Nouns:** I have retained the OCR spellings exactly (e.g., *Tratia* for Thrace, *Misia* for Moesia, *Istula* for Vistula). Note that "Ethole" in Page 199 likely refers to *Aetolia* or a corruption thereof within the context of Achaia.

# **THE SECOND OF AFRICA**
The table contains Africa [abbrev: *affricā*] and the islands which are around it. Its median parallel [abbrev: *Parallelꝰ*] has a proportion to the meridian [abbrev: *meridianū*] of [abbrev: *ꝙ*] thirteen to fifteen. The table, however [abbrev: *aūt*], is bounded: From the east by Cyrenaica; from the south by interior Libya near Getulia [abbrev: *getuliā*] and the desert [abbrev: *eremū*]; from the west by Mauritania Cesariensis; from the north by the African sea.

### **NOTABLE CITIES OF AFRICA MINOR**
* **Tabraca** has [abbrev: *hēt*] a longest day of 14 1/6 hours [abbrev: *horarꝝ*] and is distant from Alexandria [abbrev: *alexādría*] toward [abbrev: *ūsus*] the west [abbrev: *occasū*] by nearly 2 hours.
* **Ithyca** has [abbrev: *hēt*] a longest day of 14 1/4 hours [abbrev: *horarꝝ*] and is distant from Alexandria toward the west by 1 2/3 hours.

### PAGE 211

# THIRD [MAP] OF AFRICA
The third map of **Affrica** contains **Cyrenaica** [Note: printed as *Cyrenaicaycam*] and **Egyptum** with the adjacent islands. Its middle parallel has a ratio to the meridian of fifty-three to sixty. The map is bounded on the East by **iudea** and **arabia petrea** and the **arabico sinu** [Arabian Gulf]. On the South by the interior deserts of **lybia** and **ethyopia** which is below **egypto**. On the West by **affrica** and **magna syrte** [the Great Syrtis] and part of interior **lybie**. On the North by the **lybico** and **egyptio** sea.

### DISTINGUISHED CITIES OF CYRENE [CIRNES]
**Beronice**, which is also **hesperides**, has a maximal day of 14 1/2 hours and is distant from **alexandria** towards the west by 2 1/3 hours.
**Arsynoe**, which is also **theuchira**, has a maximal day of 14 1/2 hours and is distant from **alexandria** towards the west by 2 1/3 1/4 hours.
**Ptolemais** has a maximal day of 14 1/2 hours and is distant from **alexandria** towards the west by 2 3/4 hours.
**Appollonia** has a maximal day of 14 3/4 hours and is distant from **alexandria** towards the west by 3 hours.
**Cyrene** has a maximal day of 14 1/2 hours and is distant from **alexandria** towards the west by 3 hours.

### DISTINGUISHED CITIES OF MARMARICA
**Chersonesus** has a maximal day of 14 3/4 hours and is distant from **alexandria** towards [Note: *usus* for *versus*] the west by 2 1/4 hours.

### DISTINGUISHED CITIES OF LIBIA
**Paretonium** has a maximal day of 14 1/2 hours and is distant from **alexandria** towards the west by 1/4 hour.
**ALEXANDRIA** has a maximal day of 14 1/2 hours and is distant from the meridian of the **fortunatarum insularum** [Fortunate Isles] toward the rising sun [East] by 4 hours.
**Pelusium** has a maximal day of 14 1/2 hours and is distant from **alexandria** towards the east by 1/4 hour.
**Memphis** has a maximal day of 13 1/2 hours and is distant from **alexandria** towards the east by 1/8 hour.

### DISTINGUISHED CITIES OF THE THEBAID
**Ptolemais** has a maximal day of 13 2/3 hours and is distant from **alexandria** towards the east by 1/8 hour.
**Magna diopolis** has a maximal day of 13 1/2 1/8 hours and is distant from **alexandria** towards the east by 1/8 hour.

### IN THE AMMONIAC REGION
**Syene** has a maximal day of 13 1/2 hours and is distant from **alexandria** towards the east by 1/8 hour. Here, once in a year, the sun comes directly overhead when it is in the summer tropic [Solstice].
**Ammon** has a maximal day of 13 1/2 hours and is distant from **alexandria** towards the west by 1/3 hour.
**Magna oasis** has a maximal day of 13 1/3 hours and is distant from **alexandria** towards the east by 1/4 hour.
**Myformus** [Myos Hormos] has a maximal day of 13 1/2 1/4 hours and is distant from **alexandria** towards the east by 1/4 hour.
**Bernice** [Berenice] has a maximal day of 13 1/2 hours and is distant from **alexandria** towards the east by 1/4 hour. Here, once in a year, the sun comes directly overhead when it is in the summer tropic.

# FOURTH [Note: printed *VARTA* for *QVARTA*] AND LAST
map of **affrice** contains interior **lybiam** and **ethyopiam** which is below **egypto** and that which is further interior, with the islands adjacent to it. Its middle parallel has nearly the same proportion to the meridian. The map is bounded on the East by the **sinu arabico** [Arabian Gulf] and the **mari rubro** [Red Sea] and the **sinu barbarico** [Barbaric Gulf] and part of the **indici pelagi** [Indian Sea]. ### CITIES OF INTERIOR LIBYA
**Aatole** has a maximal day of 13 1/2 hours and is distant from **alexandria** towards the west by 3 1/3 hours. Here once in a year the sun comes directly overhead in the summer tropic.
**Tarzita** has a maximal day of 12 2/3 hours and is distant from **alexandria** towards the west by 3 3/4 hours. Here the sun is directly overhead twice in a year when it is distant from the summer tropic on either side by 48 3/4 degrees.
**Tamondocana** has a maximal day of 13 hours and is distant from **alexandria** towards the west by 2 3/4 hours. It receives the sun directly overhead twice in a year when it is distant from the summer tropic on either side by 43 degrees.
**Gira** has a maximal day of 13 1/2 hours and is distant from **alexandria** towards the west by 1 3/4 hours. It has the sun directly overhead twice in a year when it is distant from the summer tropic on either side by 43 degrees.
**Garame** has a maximal day of 13 hours and is distant from **alexandria** towards the west by 1 1/2 hours. Here the sun comes directly overhead twice in a year when it is distant from the summer tropic on either side by 24 degrees.

### CITIES OF ETHIOPIA BELOW EGYPT
**Nupata** has a maximal day of 13 1/4 hours and is distant from **alexandria** towards the west by 1/2 hour. Here the sun comes directly overhead twice in a year when it is distant from the summer tropic on either side by 31 1/2 degrees.

### CITIES ON THE ISLAND OF MEROE

**Adulis** has a maximal day of 12 3/4 hours and is distant from **alexandria** towards the east by 1 3/8 hours. Here the sun comes directly overhead twice in a year when it is distant from the summer tropic on either side by 62 degrees.

**Mosylu** has a maximal day of 12 1/2 hours and is distant from **alexandria** towards the east by nearly 1 1/3 hours. There the sun comes directly overhead twice in a year when it is distant from the summer tropic on either side by 68 1/2 1/4 degrees.
**Aromata** has a maximal day of 13 3/8 hours and is distant from **alexandria** towards the east by 1 1/2 hours. In these parts the sun comes directly overhead twice in a year when it is distant from the summer tropic on either side by 76 degrees.

### THE LIBYAN OR PUNIC SEA
<note>original: "Libicum sive Punicum Mare"; this refers to the stretch of the Mediterranean Sea along the coast of North Africa between Tunisia and Egypt.</note>

**Labels on the map:**

- **REGION OF CYRENAICA** <note>An ancient Greek and later Roman province in modern-day eastern Libya.</note>
- **MARMARICA AND ALL OF EGYPT** <note>Marmarica was the arid region between Cyrenaica and the Nile Delta.</note>
- **INNER LIBYA** <note>The vast interior of the African continent south of the Mediterranean coast.</note>
- **THE EGYPTIAN SEA** <note>The portion of the Mediterranean Sea bordering the Egyptian coast.</note>
- **THE ARABIAN GULF** <note>original: "Sinus Arabicus"; in ancient geography, this term referred to what we now call the Red Sea.</note>
- **The River Nile**
- **Cyrene** <note>The capital city of the Cyrenaica region, famous for its Greek ruins.</note>
- **Alexandria** <note>The great Mediterranean port and center of learning in northern Egypt.</note>
- **Memphis** <note>The ancient capital of Inebu-hedj, the first nome of Lower Egypt.</note>
- **Thebes** <note>Known to the ancient Egyptians as Waset, this was the capital of Egypt during the Middle and New Kingdoms.</note>
- **Syene** <note>Modern-day Aswan, Egypt; historically significant as the southern frontier of the Roman Empire and a key point for astronomical measurements.</note>
- **Bucolic Mountains** <note>original: "Bocolicus montes"; named for the "Bucoli" or cattle-herders who inhabited the Nile Delta and surrounding marshlands.</note>
- **Silphium-bearing region** <note>original: "Silfiofera"; Silphium was a mysterious plant, now extinct, that was highly valued in the ancient world for medicine and seasoning. It only grew in a specific strip of land in Cyrenaica.</note>
- **The Landmarks of Hercules** <note>original: "Herculis chyne"; likely referring to the altars or "sand-banks" associated with the mythical hero's travels in the desert.</note>
- **Royal Mountains** <note>original: "Basilichi montes".</note>
- **Sandy Region** <note>original: "Regio diammos"; derived from the Greek word *ammos* for sand, indicating the desert wastes of the Sahara.</note>

# THE FOURTH AND FINAL
map of Africa contains Inner Libya and Ethiopia <note>original: "ethyopiam"; in ancient geography, "Ethiopia" generally referred to all regions of Sub-Saharan Africa.</note> which is below Egypt, as well as the further interior along with its adjacent islands. Its middle parallel has nearly the same proportion to the meridian as the others. This map is bounded on the east by the Arabian Gulf <note>The Red Sea</note>, the Red Sea <note>The Indian Ocean or Erythraean Sea</note>, the Barbaric Gulf, and part of the Indian Sea. To the south, it is bounded by the unknown land and the Western Ocean <note>The Atlantic</note>. To the north, it is bounded by both Mauritanias <note>Tingitana and Caesariensis</note>, the province of Africa, Cyrenaica, and Egypt.

### CITIES OF INNER LIBYA
**Aatole** has a longest day of 13 1/2 hours and is 3 1/3 hours west of Alexandria. <note>The distance in "hours" refers to the difference in longitude; one hour represents 15 degrees of the earth's rotation.</note> Here, once a year, the sun is directly overhead <note>At the zenith</note> at the summer tropic <note>The Tropic of Cancer</note>.

**Tarzita** has a longest day of 12 2/3 hours and is 3 3/4 hours west of Alexandria. Here the sun is directly overhead twice a year when it is 48 3/4 degrees from the summer tropic on either side.

**Tamondocana** has a longest day of 13 hours and is 2 3/4 hours west of Alexandria. It receives the sun directly overhead twice a year when it is 43 degrees from the summer tropic on either side.

**Gira** <note>A significant city located near the Niger River in ancient accounts.</note> has a longest day of 13 1/2 hours and is 1 3/4 hours west of Alexandria. It has the sun directly overhead twice a year when it is 43 degrees from the summer tropic on either side.

**Garame** <note>Likely Germa, the capital of the Garamantes in modern-day Libya.</note> has a longest day of 13 hours and is 1 1/2 hours west of Alexandria. Here the sun is directly overhead twice a year when it is 24 degrees from the summer tropic on either side.

### CITIES OF ETHIOPIA BELOW EGYPT
**Napata** <note>original: "Nupata"; the capital of the Kingdom of Kush, located in modern-day Sudan.</note> has a longest day of 13 1/4 hours and is 1/2 hour west of Alexandria. Here the sun is directly overhead twice a year when it is 31 1/2 degrees from the summer tropic on either side.

### CITIES ON THE ISLAND OF MEROE
<note>Meroe was often called an "island" by ancient writers because it was bounded by the Nile, the Atbara, and the Blue Nile rivers.</note>

**Meroe** has a longest day of 13 hours and is 1 1/4 hours east of Alexandria. On it, the sun is directly overhead twice a year when it is 44 degrees from the summer tropic on either side.

**Ptolemais of the Hunts** <note>original: "Ptolemais ferarum"; a port on the Red Sea used by the Ptolemies for importing war elephants.</note> has a longest day of 13 hours and is 1 3/4 hours east of Alexandria. On it, the sun is directly overhead twice a year when it is 44 degrees from the summer tropic on either side.

**Adulis** <note>An important port city in the Kingdom of Aksum, located in modern Eritrea.</note> has a longest day of 12 3/4 hours and is 1 3/8 hours east of Alexandria. Here the sun is directly overhead twice a year when it is 62 degrees from the summer tropic on either side.

**Dera** has a longest day of 12 2/3 hours and is 1 hour east of Alexandria. It receives the sun directly overhead twice a year when it is 63 3/4 <note>represented by 1/2 and 1/4</note> degrees from the summer tropic on either side.

**Mosylu** <note>Mosylon was a prominent ancient emporium on the coast of modern-day Somalia, famous for the cinnamon trade.</note> has a longest day of 12 1/2 hours and is almost 1 1/3 hours east of Alexandria. There the sun is directly overhead twice a year when it is 68 3/4 degrees from the summer tropic on either side.

**Aromata** <note>The "Cape of Spices," identified with Cape Guardafui at the tip of the Horn of Africa.</note> has a longest day of 13 3/8 hours and is 1 1/2 hours east of Alexandria. In these parts, the sun is directly overhead twice a year when it is 76 degrees from the summer tropic on either side.

**THE FOUR MAPS OF GREATER AFRICA END HERE.**

# THE TEN MAPS OF GREATER ASIA, THE FIRST OF WHICH IS...
[[image: Historiated initial 'P' showing a geographer with a globe or astrolabe.]]
**The First Map of Asia** contains Pontus and Bithynia <note>regions in northern Asia Minor along the Black Sea</note> and the region properly called Asia <note>referring to the Roman province of Asia in western Anatolia</note>, as well as Lycia, Galatia, Pamphylia, Cappadocia, Lesser Armenia, and Cilicia <note>original: Silicia</note>. Its middle parallel has a proportion to the meridian of three to four <note>this refers to the mathematical ratio used to draw the map projection, accounting for the curvature of the Earth</note>. The map is bounded: On the East indeed by Greater Armenia and part of Syria. On the South by the Carpathian, Lycian, and Pamphylian seas, the narrows of Cilicia, and the Issic Gulf <note>the Gulf of İskenderun</note>. On the West by the Thracian Bosphorus, the Propontis <note>the Sea of Marmara</note>, the Hellespont <note>the Dardanelles</note>, the Aegean Sea, and the Icarian and Myrtoan seas. On the North by the Pontic Sea <note>The Black Sea</note>.

### THE SECOND MAP OF ASIA

# THE FOURTH MAP OF ASIA
The Fourth Map of Asia contains Cyprus, Syria, Judea, both Arabia Petrea and [Arabia] Deserta, as well as Mesopotamia and Babylonia. Its middle parallel has a proportion to the meridian of five to six. The map is bounded: on the East by Assyria, Susiana, and part of the Persian Gulf; on the South by part of the same Persian Gulf, Arabia Felix, and the inner part of the Arabian Gulf [the Red Sea]; on the West by part of Egypt, the Syriac and Pamphylian Sea, the Issic Gulf, and Cilicia; on the North by the narrows of Cilicia and part of Cappadocia and Armenia Major.

# THE FIFTH MAP OF ASIA
The Fifth Map of Asia contains Assyria, Susiana, Media, Persis, Hyrcania, Parthia, and Carmania Deserta. Its middle parallel has a proportion to the meridian of four to five. The map is bounded: on the east by Aria; on the south by Carmania and the Persian Gulf; on the west by Babylonia and Mesopotamia and part of Armenia Major; on the north by part of the Hyrcanian Sea [Caspian] and the region of Hyrcania.

**Ninos** has its longest day of 14 1/2 1/12 hours and is distant from Alexandria toward the east by 1 3/4 hours.

**Ctisiphon** has its longest day of almost 14 1/2 1/12 hours and is distant from Alexandria toward the east by 1 2/3 hours.

### FAMOUS CITIES OF SUSIANA.
**Susa** has its longest day of 14 1/3 hours and is distant from Alexandria toward the east by 1 1/2 1/12 hours.

**Scholarly Notes on Abbreviations & Fractions:**
1. **Fractions:** Renaissance geographers expressed minutes/fractions of hours by addition. E.g., "12 1/2 1/4" indicates 12 hours + 30 mins + 15 mins = 12 hours 45 mins.
2. **hē/hēt:** Abbreviations for *habet* (has/contains).
3. **hoꝛ/hoꝛar̄:** Abbreviations for *horas* or *horarum* (hours).
4. **usus/versus:** The OCR "usus" is a common misreading of "vsus," the abbreviation for *versus* (toward).
5. **pꝛeportionē:** Read as *proportionem* (the 'p' with a tail is a standard abbreviation for *pro*).
6. **ḡdib:** Abbreviation for *gradibus* (degrees).

# THE INDIAN OCEAN

<note>original: INDICVM PELAGVS. In Renaissance cartography, the term "pelagus" (from the Greek *pelagos*) refers to the deep, open sea.</note>

[This page shows the reverse side of a printed map. The ink has soaked through the paper over centuries, creating a mirrored image of the original engraving.]

<margin>
**INDIA**
</margin>

<column-break/>

->**THE INDIAN OCEAN**<-

### Map Features and Annotations
The map provides a wide view of the maritime world known to 15th and 16th-century scholars, centered on the **Indian Ocean**. Through the translucent paper, the following elements are visible:

*   **Coastlines:** Faint outlines representing the eastern coast of **Africa**, the southern coast of the **Arabian Peninsula**, and the western reaches of the **Indian subcontinent**.
*   **Numerical Scales:** Along the bottom and left margins, a border contains a scale of degrees <term>gradibus (degrees)</term> used to determine latitude and longitude. 
*   **Condition Note:** The paper exhibits significant **foxing** <note>age-related reddish-brown spots caused by mold or iron oxidation</note> and a large water stain along the upper edge, typical of volumes stored in humid historical archives.

<column-break/>

### Cartographic Context
This map likely follows the Ptolemaic tradition, which was the standard for European geography during the Renaissance. It depicts the "Indian Sea" not as a modern open ocean, but often as a large basin bounded by land to the south—a common geographical misconception of the era before the full circumnavigation of Africa was widely recorded in atlases.

<summary>This page is the reverse of a map showing the Indian Ocean, with mirrored labels for Arabia and India. It reflects the Renaissance understanding of the maritime geography connecting Africa and Asia.</summary>

The **SEVENTH MAP OF ASIA** contains Margiana, Bactria, Sogdiana, the Sacae, and Scythia within the Imaus Mountain. <note>The Imaus Mountain refers generally to the Pamir, Hindu Kush, or Himalayan ranges, which Ptolemy used as a primary divider between "Scythia within" (to the west/north) and "Scythia beyond" (to the east).</note> The middle parallel of this map has a ratio to the meridian of two to three. <note>original: "Parallelus ipsius medius pportionem habet ad meridianū quā duo ad tria." This describes the mathematical projection of the map, adjusting for the curvature of the Earth.</note> The map is bounded: On the east by Scythia within the Imaus Mountain. On the south by Mount Imaus, which is above the Indians living both within and beyond the Ganges; and further by the Paropanisadae, Aria, Parthia, and part of the Hyrcanian Sea. <note>The Hyrcanian Sea is the ancient name for the Caspian Sea.</note> On the west by the region of the Medes, the Hyrcanian Sea, and Asiatic Sarmatia. On the north by the unknown land.

Here also the sun is directly overhead once in the year, in the summer tropic itself. However, we say this because the sun is near the tropic itself. Yet it should be known that it is distant by a third part of one great degree, which in 30 [diaco?]^7 produces three degrees: and here it is necessary that the sun be directly overhead not once in the year, but twice: namely, when it is distant from the summer tropic on either side by three degrees, just as is written in the other cities which are situated in the same part of the latitude.

# TENTH MAP OF ASIA
[Note: Decorative initial **D** begins the text.]

**T**HE TENTH MAP OF ASIA contains India within the river Ganges, with the islands adjacent to it. Its middle parallel has a proportion to the meridian of eleven to twelve. Moreover, the map is circumscribed: From the east by India beyond the Ganges. From the south by the Gangetic part of the river and the Indian Sea. From the west by Gedrosia and Arachosia and the Paropanisidae. From the north by the part of the Imaus mountain which is below the Sogdiani and the Sacae.

**Symilla** has its longest day of nearly 12 1/2 1/3 1/12 hours, and is distant from Alexandria towards the east by 3 1/3. Here also the sun becomes directly overhead twice in the year, when it is distant from the summer tropic on either side by 41 3/4 degrees.
**Muzoris** has its longest day [at] 12 1/2 1/3 hours, and is distant from Alexandria towards the east by 3 3/4 hours. Here also the sun becomes directly overhead twice in the year, when it is distant from the summer tropic on either side by 42 1/2 1/4 degrees.
**Chaberis** has its longest day [at] 12 1/2 1/3 1/12 hours, or nearly 13, and is distant from Alexandria towards the east by 4 1/2 hours. Here also the sun becomes directly overhead twice in the year, when it is distant from the summer tropic on either side by 47 1/2 1/12 degrees.
**Palura** has its longest day [at] 12 2/3 1/10 hours, and is distant from Alexandria towards the east by 4 2/3 hours. Here also the sun becomes directly overhead twice in the year, when it is distant from the summer tropic on either side by 7 1/4 degrees.
**Caspira** has its longest day of nearly 14 12 hours [sic]^8, and is distant from Alexandria towards the east by nearly 4 1/2.
**Bucephala** has its longest day [at] 11 1/4 hours^9, and is distant from Alexandria towards the east by 4 1/3 3/30 hours.
**Palimbothra** has its longest day of nearly 13 1/2 1/4 hours, and is distant from Alexandria towards the east by 4 1/2 2/3 1/30.
**Patala** has its longest day of nearly 13 1/4 hours, and is distant from Alexandria towards the east by 3 1/2 1/12 hours. Here also the sun becomes directly overhead twice in the year, being distant from the summer tropic on either side by 32 1/2 1/3 degrees.
**Barbara** has its longest day [at] 13 1/2 1/12 hours, and is distant from Alexandria towards the east by 3 1/2 1/20 hours. Here also the sun becomes directly overhead twice in the year, being distant from the summer tropic on either side by 23 1/2 1/3 degrees.
**Barizaga** has its longest day [at] 13 1/12 hours, and is distant from Alexandria towards the east by 3 1/20 hours. Here also the sun becomes directly overhead twice in the year, being distant from the summer tropic on either side by 41 3/4 degrees.
**Ozena** has its longest day of nearly 13 1/4 hours, and is distant from Alexandria towards the east by 4 hours. Here also the sun becomes directly overhead twice in the year, when it is distant from the summer tropic on either side by 31 degrees.
**Bethana** has its longest day of nearly 13 1/8 hours, and is distant from Alexandria towards the east by nearly 3 2/3. Here also the sun becomes directly overhead twice in the year, being distant from the summer tropic on either side by 38 1/4 degrees.
**Hyppocura** has its longest day [at] 13 1/4 hours, and is distant from Alexandria towards the east by 4 hours. Here also the sun becomes directly overhead twice in the year, being distant from the summer tropic on either side by 34 1/3 degrees.
**Carura** has its longest day of 13 hours, and is distant from Alexandria towards the east by 3 1/2 1/3 hours. Here also the sun becomes directly overhead twice in the year, being distant from the summer tropic on either side by 49 2/3 degrees.

**Scholarly Notes on the Translation:**

1. **Imaum**: Mount Imaus (usually identifying the Himalayas or the Hindu Kush). The text on p. 251 says "citra" (this side of), though the header says "extra" (beyond).
2. **faces**: Likely a corruption or specific geographic term for the "slopes" or "aspects" (facies) of the mountain ranges.
3. **equ ho 2**: The OCR shows "equ ho 2" but the description of the 15th parallel in Ptolemy usually notes 4 hours difference from the equator to reach a 16-hour day. 
4. **Hellespont**: The text says 2 1/2 hours difference from the equinoctial; Ptolemy standardly lists 12th parallel as 15 hours longest day, but here it says 14.
5. **14 / 14 1/2**: There appears to be a numerical mismatch in the OCR'd latitude/hour tables compared to standard Ptolemaic coordinates (e.g., the 12th parallel typically has 15 hours, not 14).
6. **11. paral**: The text lists the 11th parallel as 2 hours from the equinoctial, which would result in 14 hours, but then adds 1/2 1/12. 
7. **diaco**: Possibly *diacosio* or a contraction related to the division of degrees.
8. **Caspira hours**: The OCR "14 12" is likely 14 1/2 or 14 1/12.
9. **Bucephala**: 11 1/4 hours is likely an error for 14 1/4, as it is in northern India. 
10. **Nic**: Likely a typo for "Hic" (Here).
